 Menu Home › INDUSTRY NEWS INDUSTRY NEWS Walmart Named in 81 U.S. Recalls in 2026 — More Than Any Physical Retailer
 Nov 15, 2026 Advertisement When a recall breaks, every shopper — and every buyer — asks the same thing: was it sold at my store? A new report puts hard numbers behind that instinct, and the headline figure is one that procurement directors and grocery operators will want to read carefully.
 Store Recalls , a free website that sorts official U.S. recalls by the store named in each notice, found that Walmart was named in 81 recalls between January 1 and November 10, 2026 — more than any other physical retailer. Target followed with 25 notices and Costco with 19.
 What the Data Actually Counts
 The methodology matters here, because the numbers are easy to misread. The report tallies every store mentioned across 826 recalls published by the Food and Drug Administration, the USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) and the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC). Of those, 431 notices name at least one retailer.
 Advertisement 
 Crucially, a recall is counted for a store only when the official text names the store or one of its store brands — think Great Value for Walmart or Kirkland Signature for Costco — or when the retailer posts the recall on its own recall page.
 Amazon was named in 336 notices, 306 of them CPSC recalls — most flagging products sold online at Amazon.com, often by third-party sellers.
 Food and pet food accounted for 264 of the 826 recalls.
 Undeclared allergens were the most common reason (84), followed by Salmonella (52) and Listeria (26).
 35 recalls named two or more chains at once — among them murphy beds, dressers and a cheese bread sold at four grocery chains.
 Scale, Not Safety Rating
 The report's authors are blunt about what the ranking does and doesn't mean. Larger chains sell more products and appear in more notices, so a high count reflects volume — not that a retailer is unsafe. A store not being named also doesn't mean a product was never sold there.
 "When a recall hits the news, shoppers ask one question first: was it sold at my store? The official notices often answer it, but you have to read every one to find out," said Alexandra Looks, Managing Director of Looks Einkaufs & Verwaltungs GmbH, which runs Store Recalls. "We only count a store when the notice names it, and we publish the sentence that does. A high count means a chain sells a lot, not that it is unsafe." 
 The full data set — one row per recall, with the stores named and how each was matched — is free to download under a Creative Commons Attribution license.
 Why It Matters
 For food and beverage operators, grocers and institutional buyers, the real value here isn't the leaderboard — it's the pattern. Allergens, Salmonella and Listeria dominate the food recall picture, and those are precisely the risks that supplier audits, labeling checks and cold-chain controls are built to catch.
 Advertisement 
 Practical takeaways for the industry:
 Treat undeclared allergens as a top-tier labeling risk. They outranked every pathogen in 2026 recall volume. Tighten spec reviews and private-label artwork approvals accordingly.
 Watch the store-brand exposure. Recalls that name Great Value or Kirkland Signature show how private-label programs put a retailer's name directly on the notice — a reputational factor worth building into supplier contracts.
 Don't confuse frequency with risk. As the report stresses, volume drives counts. Use the underlying, freely downloadable data to trace specific products and suppliers rather than ranking chains.
 Mind the online marketplace gap. Amazon's 336 mentions — overwhelmingly third-party CPSC cases — are a reminder that marketplace sellers can expose a platform to recall notices in ways that differ from traditional retail buying.
 For procurement teams, a resource that quotes the exact sentence naming a store turns a vague "is this ours?" scramble into a faster, documentable answer — useful for crisis response, recall withdrawals and customer communication alike.
 Food safety and supply-chain resilience continue to shape the conversations driving global food events , and the cybersecurity of retail infrastructure is adding a new layer of risk — as seen when refrigeration cyberattacks hit European supermarkets .
 The Bottom Line
 The 2026 Store Recalls report is less a verdict on any one retailer than a mirror held up to the entire supply chain. For operators, the smart move is to mine the data for the trends that map to your own risk — allergens, pathogens, private-label exposure — and sharpen your controls before a notice ever reaches your shelves.
